analysis.one_liner: Freezes federal designation of new wetlands until a new farm law is enacted.
analysis.headline: The bill to freeze federal wetland designations, backed by an Iowa Republican and 22 cosponsors, never got a vote and died in committee after the Agriculture Department issued an unfavorable review.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred the Agriculture Department, the Army, and the EPA from designating any new wetlands until Congress passed a new farm law to replace the 1990 farm bill. Those designations are what trigger restrictions on draining or filling wetlands under farm programs and Clean Water Act permits. In practice, a freeze would have let landowners proceed without new federal wetland limits, while the public lost the flood control and water-cleaning functions those designations protect. It never advanced out of committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Farm landowners and developers who wanted to drain, fill, or crop land that might be designated a wetland. With no new delineations, fewer properties would have become subject to swampbuster penalties under farm programs or Clean Water Act section 404 permits, at least until a successor farm law passed.

how_it_helps.text: It barred the Secretary of Agriculture, the Secretary of the Army, and the EPA Administrator from delineating wetlands under the 1985 farm bill's wetland conservation (swampbuster) subtitle and Clean Water Act section 404, the permit program for filling wetlands.
During the moratorium, landowners could drain, fill, or crop land without new federal wetland designations triggering restrictions or permit requirements on that land.
The moratorium had no fixed end date: it ran until enactment of a successor to the 1990 farm law, so it could have lasted for years.

analysis.who_pays: The public, through weakened wetland protection. New delineations are how the government identifies wetlands that buffer floods, filter water, and provide habitat; freezing them under the Clean Water Act permit program would have allowed filling of wetlands with less federal review. Landowners were also left in limbo, since restrictions could resume the moment a successor farm law passed.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public near wetlands and waterways

drawbacks.text: The U.S. Department of Agriculture opposed the bill, delivering an unfavorable executive comment to the House in October 1995.

Freezing delineations under Clean Water Act section 404 would have let wetlands be filled with no new federal review, sacrificing the flood control, water filtration, and habitat benefits wetlands provide to surrounding communities.

The bill suspended the rules without replacing them, leaving landowners uncertain: everything could snap back as soon as a successor farm law was enacted, and anyone who altered land in the meantime might face retroactive problems.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered landowners relief from new wetland restrictions, but it was a blunt pause rather than a reform: it stopped the government from even identifying wetlands, without changing the underlying rules, and the Agriculture Department weighed in against it. The costs fell on the public's flood protection and water quality, which is why it drew no momentum even in a Congress controlled by the sponsor's own party.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and their subcommittees, drew an unfavorable review from the Agriculture Department, and never received a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Tom Latham of Iowa introduced the bill on March 13, 1995, and it was referred to both the Agriculture Committee and the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee.
Within two weeks it was sent to subcommittees in both committees, and the House asked the U.S. Department of Agriculture for its views.
On October 3, 1995, USDA delivered an unfavorable executive comment, and no further action was ever taken on the bill.
The bill died when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997, without ever reaching the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal wetland protections stayed intact, and the public kept the flood-buffering and water-cleaning benefits that come with them. Landowners hoping to convert wetlands without new designations got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal wetland protections and the public

for.name: Rep. Tom Latham
for.what_they_did: Introduced the moratorium bill and recruited cosponsors for it.

for.name: 22 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 22 cosponsors were Republicans.

against.name: House Agriculture and Transportation & Infrastructure Committees
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to subcommittees and never reported it out, so it never reached the House floor.

against.name: U.S. Department of Agriculture
against.what_they_did: Delivered an unfavorable executive comment on the bill in October 1995.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 22 cosponsors were Republicans, but the bill never got a vote, so the partisan split was never tested.

industries.industry: Agricultural landowners (row-crop and livestock farms near wetlands)
industries.note: The bill's main beneficiaries: a freeze on new wetland delineations would have kept their land from being designated under swampbuster, letting them drain or crop it without those restrictions. The public's flood protection and water quality would absorb the cost.
Clean Water Act section 404 permits for filling wetlands are a key hurdle for builders; freezing new delineations would have removed that hurdle for newly identified wetlands during the moratorium.
Agencies barred from delineating wetlands would order far fewer delineations, cutting work for firms that perform them. Their interest runs with the public's in stronger wetland protection.
